shot1: Shot 1 begins with a fade-in from black, using a wide-angle slightly overhead composition. The edge of a broken skyscraper occupies the left foreground, with layers of collapsed city ruins and a wind-swept horizon in the background. Gray daylight evenly illuminates from above, casting cold, fragmented pixelated reflections on the metal surface. A faint backlight outlines its sharp silhouette. It slowly contracts and lowers its center of gravity against the surface, showing subtle ripples and inward pulsations. Then, thin, taut wing membranes extend from both sides, fluttering under strong wind pressure. Loose stones beneath it roll backward as if sucked away. The The camera first makes a very slight push-in, then horizontally tracks along the edge, clearly foreshadowing the imminent leap.
shot2: Shot 2 enters abruptly with a hard cut into high-speed action, using a medium-wide eye-level tracking shot. The frame instantly connects to the subject’s sudden leap from the edge. Foreground elements include broken rebar and wall fragments rushing past. In mid-ground, the liquid metal sphere rapidly deploys full wing membranes during descent. The background reveals a long, narrow ruin canyon stretching forward, with strong perspective lines compressing the sense of speed. Lighting remains consistent cold-gray natural light. As it flies, the metal surface reflects shifting dark and bright patterns from passing debris. Traditional cloth-like physical follow-up is replaced by membrane fluttering, stretching, and recoil. The liquid body elongates slightly under airflow, then lowers and speeds through rubble and cracked roads. It completes two consecutive rolls to avoid obstacles: first gliding just beneath a twisted steel beam spanning the canyon, then side-rolling to dodge an approaching concrete overhang. Its flight path closely follows terrain undulations, trailing fine dust streaks from its rear. The camera initially dives downward to follow, then quickly pushes forward, briefly panning sideways to keep the subject centered.
shot3: Shot 3 transitions via a hard cut masked by rising dust from the previous shot, entering a close-up slightly low-angle dynamic shot. The foreground shows swirling sand curtains and blurred turbine blade remnants speeding past. The mid-ground tightly frames the liquid metal sphere, while the background features two toppled turbines and a hazy wasteland horizon forming a claustrophobic passage. The main light source remains filtered cold daylight from the storm. Scattered backlight within the dust creates thin glowing edges on the wing membranes, enhancing pixel grain and danger atmosphere. As the subject enters the storm, its outline momentarily blurs. The liquid surface is torn into flowing textures by the wind. It then corrects its posture through extremely subtle wing membrane adjustments—expansion, curvature changes, and angle shifts—first hugging one side of a broken turbine support, then sharply retracting inward to squeeze through the gap between two damaged blades and twisted cables. At the moment of passage, the body nearly grazes the metal edges, and its reflective surface fractures into rapidly flickering gray-white shards. Pattering gravel hits on the membranes increase tension. The camera performs a short arc around the subject before quickly pulling back, emphasizing regained stability after peril.
shot4: Shot 4 connects naturally as dust thins out, using a wide-to-medium close-up overhead diving shot. Foreground elements include scattered dust particles being flung off. Below in mid-ground appears the massive skeletal antenna of a crashed satellite. The background shows a wind-eroded, nearly still wasteland plain with scattered wreckage. The antenna’s curved structure provides a clear landing point and guides visual focus. The dominant cool-gray tone remains consistent. After breaking through the dust, light becomes slightly clearer but retains overcast quality. Reflections on the antenna’s metal edges echo those on the subject’s surface. The liquid metal sphere transitions from stable gliding after the tight passage into a dive, gradually narrowing its wing membranes to reduce drag. Near the antenna, it first extends into a streamlined shape, then sharply retracts inward, landing precisely on the tilted antenna tip. Upon contact, the liquid body briefly spreads like mercury, then rapidly reforms into a compact sphere. Remaining wing membranes retract and vanish, leaving only fine dust trails along the antenna frame and a ripple of residual wind vibration. The camera follows the dive, then gently pulls back and tilts upward to stop, keeping the subject firmly centered, completing a full action loop from gathering force, leaping, avoiding obstacles, to final landing.
